blocks.text: Where the condos are and what to know

items.t: Fairfield Island is a residential neighbourhood in the City of Chilliwack, BC, north of Chilliwack Proper.

Fairfield Island is part of the City's Chilliwack Proper and Fairfield Island Neighbourhood Plan (Schedule B2 of the Chilliwack 2050 Official Community Plan, Bylaw No. 5500). The Sardis plan is Schedule B5 and the Agricultural Area Plan Schedule B1 of the same bylaw.
Municipality: City of Chilliwack, BC. Nearby area: Chilliwack Proper to the south, with which it shares the Schedule B2 neighbourhood plan.
Where the condos are: there aren't any apartment condos here.
The City plans the area (Schedule B2, with Chilliwack Proper).

A detached house here can still come with a strata fee. The Williams Road example sits in a 6-unit bare-land strata described in its listing as carrying a minimal fee — a buyer who assumes "detached = no strata" misses the corporation, its bylaws and its Form B entirely.
The flood question is open. A seller's reassurance is not a substitute for the City's own parcel check.

The plan name surprises people: Fairfield Island doesn't have its own plan. It's covered by the joint "Chilliwack Proper and Fairfield Island Neighbourhoods Plan", so a search for "Fairfield Island" alone misses documents under Chilliwack Proper.

Rule changes that affect bare-land strata lots here: rental bans void from November 24, 2022; more 55+ exemptions from May 1, 2023; at least 10% of the budget into the reserve from November 1, 2023; depreciation reports every five years from July 1, 2024; and Chilliwack's small-scale housing bylaw (5395) adopted June 18, 2024.

blocks.text: A home on ALR land can't be stratified, so the acreages on the north and east edges are freehold farm and residential land, never townhouses.
Where the townhomes are and what to know

items.t: Board identity and numbers: Chilliwack is a CADREB market, not a Fraser Valley or Greater Vancouver board market, and is not covered by SnapStats, so SnapStats figures do not apply to this area.

Chilliwack property taxes: notices are mailed at the end of May and taxes are due the first working day after July 1. A 5% penalty applied to 2026 taxes unpaid after July 2, 2026, and another 5% to taxes unpaid after August 4, 2026. Fairfield Island is inside the City of Chilliwack, so the regional district's rural tax dates (October 31) don't apply.

It's a slough, not the Fraser River, that makes this an island day to day. The neighbourhood plan says Fairfield Island is separated from the rest of Chilliwack Proper by the Hope Slough and is reached only by the road bridges at Menzies Road and Young Road, with a pedestrian and cycling bridge planned at Williams Street. Every trip to the hospital or downtown crosses one of those two bridges.

The plan expects infill, not a townhouse project. The Schedule B-2 framework addresses infill development opportunities — redevelopment of existing large lots into smaller-lot single detached, duplex or row housing, some convenience commercial, and new attached housing along Hope River Road — and notes there are limited commercial services within the neighbourhood at present.

The City's own plan describes the homes here: mostly one- and two-storey detached houses from the 1970s and 1980s. So you're buying a house of that age, and need a home inspection to match, not a strata home with a depreciation report.

blocks.text: Lots and land in Fairfield Island

items.t: Fee-simple lots are the norm: detached single-family houses on flat lots, ranchers, custom homes by the river, and ALR acreages on the north and east edges.
Bare-land strata: some detached houses on Fairfield Island are on bare-land strata lots. A listing line saying "no other restrictions" isn't the strata's registered bylaws; read those in the Form B.
No ALR split figure for the neighbourhood is published, so none is stated.
Check the property's flood position with the City before you make an offer; it's a must here.

blocks.text: Where lots come up and what to know

items.t: Development Permit Areas in the OCP's Schedule D, as named on the City page: D-1 Drinking Water Supply, D-2 Hillside Environment, D-3 Riparian Area, D-4 Farm Home Plate, D-5 Hillside Development, D-6 Downtown, D-7 Mixed-Use Areas, D-8 Residential, D-9 Commercial, D-10 Industrial.

On the Agricultural Land Reserve land at the north and east edges: subdividing, a new house, coach house or suite, fill or soil removal, and non-farm uses may need Agricultural Land Commission approval, and ALR homes can't be stratified. The main house can be up to 500 m² with a suite only inside it, plus one additional home of up to 90 m² on parcels of 40 ha or less, or 186 m² on larger ones. Homes must also meet the City's farm home plate rules, or need a development permit. For farm tax status, you need farm income of $10,000 on under 0.8 ha, $2,500 on 0.8–4 ha, or $2,500 plus 5% of the land value over 4 ha on larger properties, with applications due by October 31. Check a property's ALR status on the City's Webmap.
For flood questions, start with the City directly.
A detached house here can still be a strata purchase. Title, not appearance, decides whether a Form B, strata fees and bylaws come with the lot.

The neighbourhood plan is shared, not standalone. Fairfield Island has no plan of its own: it is planned jointly with Chilliwack Proper as Schedule B2 of Bylaw 5500 — a buyer reading only a "Fairfield Island plan" would be reading the wrong document.

Where the acreages are and what to know

items.t: Identity: Fairfield Island is a residential neighbourhood in the City of Chilliwack, north of Chilliwack Proper, working to Young Road North, Menzies Road, Hope River Road, Clare Avenue, Bell Road and Ballam Road. The City's OCP page confirms the planning identity: Schedule B2 is the "Chilliwack Proper and Fairfield Island Neighbourhoods Plan" — a named neighbourhood-plan area grouped with Chilliwack Proper.

The plan name does quiet work: Fairfield Island does not have its own neighbourhood plan — it is planned jointly with Chilliwack Proper under Schedule B2, so the document a buyer should read for this area covers the older city core as well, and "Fairfield Island policy" usually means a B2 passage written for both areas at once.

The perimeter is a different legal world from the interior: Two streets apart, a Fairfield Island parcel can move from flat-lot residential ground into ALR ground where a house plan triggers the Farm Home Plate permit area, the ALC residence caps and the no-stratification rule — the split is per-parcel on the City Webmap, not visible from the street.

faq.a: They can where a parcel is in the Agricultural Land Reserve — the northern and eastern perimeter acreages are the exposure. ALR properties are subject to the Agricultural Land Commission Act and regulations, and an ALC application may be required for a new house, coach house or suite, fill or soil removal, a non-farm use, or a subdivision or boundary adjustment; check a parcel on the City Webmap. An ALR residence also cannot be stratified.
faq.q: Can ALR rules affect a Fairfield Island property?

faq.a: Suites and secondary units (Zoning Bylaw No. 5000): a secondary suite can be up to 90 m² or 40% of the home, whichever is smaller; one secondary unit is allowed per lot; and garden suites can be up to 100 m². The small-scale housing amendment (Bylaw 5395, adopted June 18, 2024) allows more units on eligible lots. Check a specific lot with the City.

faq.a: Pad rent under the tenancy agreement, plus the home's tax and insurance. A Fairfield Island bare-land strata owner pays a strata fee instead — there is no pad rent.

faq.a: If a half duplex comes up, check the title first: a strata half comes with a Form B for its two-lot strata, while a fee-simple half is its own lot with registered party-wall agreements. I don't know of either on the island today.
